name: Chen Ning Yang
did: While a professor at Stony Brook (1966–1999) he pursued scientific and educational relationships between the US and China, then moved back to Tsinghua University in 2003 to develop theoretical physics in China.
caveat: Nobel Prize in Physics 1957 (with T.D. Lee). Died 18 October 2025 per the Nobel Foundation.

name: Tsung-Dao Lee
did: Founded the China-U.S. Physics Examination and Application (CUSPEA) program, which sent Chinese students to US graduate schools and helped train 915 doctoral students.
caveat: Nobel Prize in Physics 1957; Columbia University professor. Died in San Francisco in 2024.

name: Samuel C. C. Ting
did: Leads the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS-02) on the International Space Station, a ~56-institute, 16-country collaboration in which China's Institute of High Energy Physics and Sun Yat-sen University (which built the tracker thermal control system) take part.
caveat: Born in Ann Arbor, Michigan, to Chinese parents and raised in China and Taiwan; MIT professor; Nobel Prize in Physics 1976.

name: Shing-Tung Yau
did: After decades as a Harvard professor (from 1987, emeritus 2022) he returned full-time to Tsinghua University in 2022, where he directs the Yau Mathematical Sciences Center and is founding president of the Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications.
caveat: Born in Shantou in 1949 and raised in Hong Kong; Fields Medal 1982. The 2022 full-time return is confirmed by Tsinghua University news.

name: Andrew Chi-Chih Yao
did: Resigned a tenured Princeton professorship to join Tsinghua University full-time in 2004 and in 2005 set up the Computer Science Experimental Class ('Yao Class') with Microsoft Research Asia.
caveat: Born in Shanghai and raised in Taiwan; Turing Award 2000. Later renounced US citizenship.

name: Yo-Yo Ma
did: Founded the Silk Road Project in 1998 to bring together musicians from different traditions, including Chinese musicians, in cross-cultural collaboration.
caveat: Born in Paris to Chinese parents and raised in the US. Listed by the Committee of 100 (founded 1990 to foster positive US–China relations) among its first members. Contribution is cultural rather than measured in numbers.

name: I. M. Pei
did: The Chinese-born US architect designed the Fragrant Hill Hotel in Beijing (opened 1982), the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong (1982–1989) and the Suzhou Museum (2000–2006).
caveat: Born in Guangzhou in 1917. Per the Committee of 100, he founded that group in 1990 to foster positive US–China relations and used his Pritzker Prize money to fund scholarships for Chinese architecture students.

name: John Leighton Stuart
did: First president of Yenching University in Beijing and US ambassador to China (1946–1949); his ashes were interred near his childhood home in Hangzhou in November 2008.
src: Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training
caveat: Born in Hangzhou to American missionary parents. Criticised in Mao Zedong's 1949 essay 'Farewell, Leighton Stuart!'; his record is judged differently in China and the US.

name: Pearl S. Buck
did: Raised in China by missionary parents and living there until 1934, she wrote novels about Chinese rural life that won the 1938 Nobel Prize in Literature, and she founded Welcome House to arrange adoptions of Asian-American children.
caveat: Her portrayals of China were later criticised by some Chinese writers.

name: George Hatem (Ma Haide)
did: The American physician went to Shanghai in 1933, stayed in China for the rest of his life, and is widely credited with eliminating most syphilis and gonorrhea in the country while campaigning against leprosy.
caveat: Born in Buffalo, New York, to Lebanese immigrants. He worked closely with the Chinese Communist Party leadership from the 1930s.

name: Kai-Fu Lee
did: Led Microsoft's first Asian research lab, opened in Beijing in 1998 (now Microsoft Research Asia), which began with five employees and a planned investment of about US$80 million over six years.
caveat: Born in Taipei, Taiwan, and educated in the US; later a venture investor in China (Sinovation Ventures).

name: Fei-Fei Li
did: As Chief Scientist of Google AI she announced and co-led the Google AI China Center in Beijing, Google's first AI research center in Asia, in December 2017.
caveat: Born in Beijing; moved to the US at 16 (per AWIS). Google says the center was disbanded about two years later.

name: Jon Huntsman Jr.
did: Served as US ambassador to China (credentials 28 Aug 2009 to Apr 2011) and later to Russia (Oct 2017 to Oct 2019).
src: US Department of State, Office of the Historian

name: George H. W. Bush
did: Headed the US Liaison Office in Beijing for about 15 months (1974–1975), before full diplomatic relations, and as president kept engaging China after 1989.
src: George H.W. Bush Foundation for U.S.-China Relations
caveat: His handling of US–China relations after June 1989 was debated in the US.

name: J. Stapleton Roy
did: Served as US ambassador to China from August 1991 to June 1995, after earlier posts including ambassador to Singapore.
src: US Department of State, Office of the Historian

name: Hu Shih
did: Earned a Columbia doctorate under John Dewey (1917), interpreted for Dewey's 1919 lecture tour of China, and as Chinese ambassador to the US (1938–1942) rallied American support during the Japanese invasion.
caveat: Republic of China (Nationalist) diplomat; later led Academia Sinica in Taiwan.

name: Ji Chaozhu
did: Educated in the US (including Harvard) before returning to China, he served for years as an interpreter for Chinese leaders, became ambassador to the UK, and was UN Under-Secretary-General from 1991 to 1995.
caveat: China Daily records him as chief Chinese interpreter during Nixon's February 1972 visit.

name: Isaac Stern
did: Toured China in 1979 with concerts and master classes in Beijing, Shanghai and Xi'an; the tour became the Academy Award-winning documentary 'From Mao to Mozart: Isaac Stern in China'.
caveat: Born in 1920 in Kremenets (then Poland, now Ukraine); raised in San Francisco.

name: Glenn Cowan
did: His April 1971 encounter with Zhuang Zedong at the World Table Tennis Championships in Japan preceded China's invitation to the US team, an opening that led to Kissinger's secret trip that July.
caveat: Whether the encounter was spontaneous is disputed; Kissinger believed Chinese players had instructions to befriend Americans.

name: Zhuang Zedong
did: The three-time world table tennis champion greeted American player Glenn Cowan with a gift in April 1971, an encounter followed by China's invitation to the US team ('ping-pong diplomacy').
caveat: Later became China's sports minister during the Cultural Revolution and was detained after 1976.

name: Yao Ming
did: The No. 1 pick in the 2002 NBA draft played eight seasons for the Houston Rockets and is credited with linking the NBA to China; he was elected to the Basketball Hall of Fame in 2016.
caveat: Later elected president of the Chinese Basketball Association (2017).

name: Henry Kissinger
did: Made a secret trip to Beijing on 9–11 July 1971 whose talks with Premier Zhou Enlai produced the agreement for President Nixon's February 1972 visit to China.
caveat: Born in Fürth, Germany. A controversial figure: his policies on Vietnam, Cambodia, Chile and East Pakistan (1971) are widely criticised, and his later China consulting drew scrutiny.

name: Zhang Yongzhen
did: His Fudan University team sequenced SARS-CoV-2 and he sent the genome to Edward Holmes, who posted it publicly on virological.org at 01:05 on 11 January 2020, the first public release.
caveat: A global rather than bilateral contribution; partner Holmes is UK-born and Sydney-based. GISAID claims an earlier release, which the cited article disputes.

name: Edward C. Holmes
did: Posted the SARS-CoV-2 genome sequenced by Zhang Yongzhen's Fudan University team on virological.org on 11 January 2020, making it publicly available worldwide.
caveat: UK-born; based at the University of Sydney (Australia is not one of the listed powers).

name: Yuan Longping
did: The 'Father of Hybrid Rice' helped triple China's rice output within about a generation; his methods spread across Asia, Africa and the Americas, and he shared the 2004 World Food Prize.
caveat: The cited source does not name specific adopting countries; the US link reflects the US-based World Food Prize rather than residence.

name: Billy Graham
did: On a 1988 tour of China (Beijing, Nanjing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and his wife Ruth's childhood home) he met Premier Li Peng and other leaders.
caveat: He also preached in the USSR (1982, 1984), which is not covered by the cited page; his 1982 Moscow remarks were criticised in the US as naive about religious freedom there.

name: Wassily Leontief
did: The Russian-born Harvard economist received the 1973 Nobel Prize for developing the input-output method and applying it to important economic problems.
caveat: The Nobel Foundation gives his birthplace as St Petersburg; some later research suggests he was born in Munich and raised in St Petersburg.

name: Simon Kuznets
did: The Harvard economist received the 1971 Nobel Prize for his empirically founded interpretation of economic growth, work behind modern national income accounting.
caveat: Born in Pinsk, Russian Empire, now Belarus.

name: Igor Sikorsky
did: After building the first four-engine airplane in Russia (1913) he emigrated in 1919 and in the US created the VS-300 (1939), the model for modern single-rotor helicopters.
caveat: Born in Kyiv, Russian Empire, now Ukraine.

name: Vladimir Zworykin
did: Emigrated from Russia in 1919 and as director of RCA's Electronic Research Lab developed the kinescope and the storage principle underlying modern television.
caveat: Born in Murom, Russia.

name: Alexei Abrikosov
did: The Moscow-born physicist moved to Argonne National Laboratory and shared the 2003 Nobel Prize for pioneering contributions to the theory of superconductors and superfluids.

name: George Balanchine
did: The St Petersburg-trained choreographer co-founded the School of American Ballet (1934) and New York City Ballet (1948) with Lincoln Kirstein, creating some 465 works.
caveat: Of Georgian descent; born in St Petersburg in 1904.

name: Mikhail Baryshnikov
did: After leaving the USSR in 1974 he became artistic director of American Ballet Theatre (1980–1989) and founded the Baryshnikov Arts Center in New York in 2005.
caveat: Born in Riga, Latvian SSR (now Latvia, an EU member state). He defected rather than being sent abroad, and has criticised Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

name: Mstislav Rostropovich
did: Music director of the US National Symphony Orchestra for 17 years from 1977, he led it on a 1990 tour to Moscow, after which his Soviet citizenship (revoked in 1978) was restored.
src: Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training
caveat: Born in Baku, Azerbaijan SSR (now Azerbaijan). He left the USSR after supporting dissidents.

name: Van Cliburn
did: Won the first International Tchaikovsky Competition in Moscow in 1958 at the height of the Cold War, becoming a celebrity in both countries; Russia awarded him the Order of Friendship in 2004.

name: Albert Sabin
did: Because the US had not approved large field trials, his oral polio vaccine was tested in the Soviet Union, where 77 million people were vaccinated between 1959 and 1961, results that led to US licensing in 1961.
caveat: Born in Białystok, Russian Empire (now Poland); US citizen. Soviet partner Mikhail Chumakov is not named in this source.

name: Viktor Zhdanov
did: As Soviet Deputy Health Minister he told the 1958 World Health Assembly that global smallpox eradication was feasible, and the USSR offered WHO 25 million doses of vaccine; the global programme was adopted in 1959.
caveat: Multilateral (WHO) rather than strictly US–USSR; paired with D.A. Henderson's US-led campaign.

name: D. A. Henderson
did: Directed WHO's global smallpox eradication campaign from Geneva from 1966; the last natural case occurred in 1977 and WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.
src: Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health
caveat: The campaign relied heavily on Soviet-donated vaccine; the US–USSR link is through WHO rather than bilateral.

name: Siegfried Hecker
did: As director of Los Alamos he led US scientists to the closed Russian nuclear city of Sarov in February 1992, starting 'lab-to-lab' cooperation that lasted almost 25 years.
caveat: Born in 1943 in German-occupied Poland and raised in Austria before emigrating to the US.

name: Sam Nunn
did: Co-sponsored the Nunn-Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction program, which by November 2010 had deactivated 7,599 strategic nuclear warheads and destroyed 791 ICBMs in former Soviet states.
caveat: Figures cover Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan, not Russia alone. DTRA cites 'more than 7,500' warheads.

name: Richard Lugar
did: Co-sponsored the Nunn-Lugar Cooperative Threat Reduction program, which by November 2010 had deactivated 7,599 strategic nuclear warheads and destroyed 791 ICBMs in former Soviet states.
caveat: Figures cover Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan, not Russia alone.

name: Thomas Stafford
did: Commanded the US side of the 1975 Apollo-Soyuz docking; his Soviet counterpart Alexei Leonov became a close friend, and Stafford gave Leonov's eulogy at his 2019 state funeral.

name: Alexei Leonov
did: Led the Soviet side of the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project, whose Soyuz docked with Apollo on 17 July 1975, where he and Thomas Stafford shook hands in orbit.
caveat: First person to walk in space (1965).

name: Anatoly Dobrynin
did: As Soviet ambassador in Washington for 24 years he dealt with six US presidents and helped defuse the 1962 Cuban missile crisis.

name: Jack F. Matlock Jr.
did: Served as US ambassador to the Soviet Union from April 1987 to August 1991, the final years of the Cold War.
src: US Department of State, Office of the Historian

name: William J. Burns
did: Served as US ambassador to Russia from November 2005 to May 2008, among other senior diplomatic posts.
src: US Department of State, Office of the Historian
caveat: Later served as CIA Director (2021–2025).

name: Suzanne Massie
did: The writer on Russian culture met President Reagan about 20 times from 1984 and taught him the Russian proverb 'trust, but verify', which he used often in arms-control talks.
caveat: Exact meeting count varies by account (18–22).

name: Mikhail Gorbachev
did: Awarded the 1990 Nobel Peace Prize 'for the leading role he played in the radical changes in East-West relations', including détente with the US.
caveat: His legacy is viewed very differently in Russia, where many associate him with the Soviet collapse and economic hardship.

name: Joseph Rotblat
did: The Warsaw-born physicist, who worked on the atomic bomb at Liverpool and Los Alamos, was Secretary-General (1957–1973) and later President of the Pugwash Conferences, which brought together scientists from East and West; Nobel Peace Prize 1995.
caveat: Born in Poland (now an EU member state); British citizen from 1946.

name: Nikita (Iakinf) Bichurin
did: Headed the Ninth Russian Ecclesiastical Mission in Beijing for about 14 years (to 1821), studying Chinese and Manchu texts, and became regarded as a founding father of Russian sinology.
src: Institute of Oriental Manuscripts, RAS (I. Popova)
caveat: Born in Chuvashia (Russia). He was later exiled to Valaam monastery for neglecting his missionary duties.

name: Vasily M. Alekseyev
did: Made research trips to China in 1906–1909, 1912 and 1926 (including Chavannes' 1907 expedition), translated Chinese literature, and trained a generation of Soviet sinologists as an Academician.

name: Konstantin S. Silin
did: Led a group of 28 Soviet bridge specialists who gave technical guidance on the Wuhan Yangtze River Bridge, the first bridge over the main Yangtze, opened in 1957.
caveat: Years of his stay are not given precisely in the source.

name: Wang Ganchang
did: Working at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna, USSR, from 1956, he led the discovery of the anti-sigma-minus hyperon in 1959.
caveat: Later a leader of China's nuclear weapons program.

name: Mei Lanfang
did: Toured Moscow and Leningrad from February to April 1935, exchanging ideas with Stanislavski, Meyerhold and Eisenstein, whose work later drew on Peking opera.

name: Ge Baoquan
did: The translator of Pushkin and Gorky worked in Moscow as a journalist and, after 1949, took over China's embassy in the USSR as chargé d'affaires; Moscow State University gave him an honorary doctorate in 1987.

name: Xian Xinghai
did: The Macau-born composer went to the USSR in 1940 to study and work, composing symphonies and the 'Chinese Rhapsody' there before dying in Moscow in 1945.
caveat: Bridge role is cultural rather than diplomatic.

name: Matteo Ricci
did: The Italian Jesuit spent 28 years in China, printed the first world map in Chinese (Kunyu Wanguo Quantu, 1602) and died in Beijing in 1610.

name: Xu Guangqi
did: Spent four years with Matteo Ricci translating the first six books of Euclid's Elements into Chinese (printed 1607).
caveat: Ming scholar-official and Catholic convert; never travelled to Europe.

name: Joseph Needham
did: Set up the Sino-British Science Co-operation Office in wartime Chongqing (1942–1946) and launched 'Science and Civilisation in China', now 25 published parts.
caveat: Investigated 1952 allegations of US germ warfare in Korea and endorsed them, which damaged his standing in the West.

name: Charles K. Kao
did: The Shanghai-born engineer at Standard Telecommunication Laboratories in Harlow, UK, made groundbreaking achievements in transmitting light in fibres for optical communication (Nobel Prize 2009).
caveat: Later Vice-Chancellor of the Chinese University of Hong Kong; held UK and US citizenship.

name: Xuanzang
did: Left Chang'an in 627, studied at Nalanda for about five years, returned in 644 with 657 Buddhist texts, and translated 75 works in 1,335 fascicles.

name: Dwarkanath Kotnis
did: One of five doctors in the Indian medical mission sent to China during the war against Japan, he worked at the Bethune International Peace Hospital and died in China on 9 December 1942, aged 32.
src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the PRC
caveat: He served with Communist forces in northern China.

name: Rabindranath Tagore
did: Visited China in April 1924 at the invitation of the Beijing Lecture Association, and in 1937 co-founded Cheena Bhavana (Chinese studies) at Visva-Bharati with Tan Yun-shan.
caveat: His 1924 lectures met protests from some Chinese intellectuals. His visits to Japan (1916, 1924, 1929) are well known but not covered by the cited source.

name: Tan Yunshan
did: Co-founded Cheena Bhavana, the Department of Chinese at Visva-Bharati University in Santiniketan, with Rabindranath Tagore on 14 April 1937.

name: Jianzhen (Ganjin)
did: After about five failed attempts over 12 years, the Tang monk reached Japan in 753, set up an ordination platform at Tōdai-ji, gave precepts to Emperor Shōmu, and founded Tōshōdai-ji.
caveat: Traditional accounts say he went blind during his attempts.

name: Shuji Nakamura
did: Developed efficient blue LEDs in Japan (Nobel Prize 2014) and immigrated to the US in 1999 to teach engineering at UC Santa Barbara.
caveat: Became a US citizen; his lawsuit against former employer Nichia over invention rewards was widely publicised in Japan.

name: Syukuro Manabe
did: Moved from Japan to the US Weather Bureau (later NOAA's GFDL) in 1959, built early climate models (Nobel Prize 2021), and led global warming research in Japan in 1997–2001.

name: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar
did: Studied and held a fellowship at Cambridge (1930–1937), then joined the University of Chicago in 1937, where his work on stellar structure won the 1983 Nobel Prize.
caveat: Born in Lahore, British India (now Pakistan).

name: Har Gobind Khorana
did: At the University of Wisconsin he shared the 1968 Nobel Prize for interpreting the genetic code and its function in protein synthesis.
caveat: The Nobel Foundation lists Raipur, India; most biographies place his birthplace in Punjab, in present-day Pakistan.

name: Venki Ramakrishnan
did: Born in Chidambaram, India, he worked in the US and then at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, UK, sharing the 2009 Nobel Prize for studies of the ribosome.
caveat: President of the Royal Society 2015–2020.

name: Andre Geim
did: The Sochi-born physicist, at the University of Manchester after working in the Netherlands, shared the 2010 Nobel Prize for groundbreaking experiments on graphene.
caveat: Holds Dutch and British citizenship.

name: Konstantin Novoselov
did: The Nizhny Tagil-born physicist shared the 2010 Nobel Prize with Andre Geim at the University of Manchester for groundbreaking experiments on graphene.
caveat: Earlier worked in the Netherlands; later moved to the National University of Singapore.

name: Ilya Prigogine
did: The Moscow-born chemist, at the Université Libre de Bruxelles and the University of Texas, won the 1977 Nobel Prize for non-equilibrium thermodynamics and the theory of dissipative structures.

name: John Rabe
did: The German Siemens manager, in China for 30 years, helped organise the Nanking Safety Zone in 1937–1938, which sheltered some 200,000 Chinese civilians.
caveat: He was a Nazi Party member; Allied authorities declared him de-Nazified in 1946.

name: Edwin O. Reischauer
did: As US ambassador to Japan (1961–1966) he pursued an 'equal partnership' between the two countries, and he founded Harvard's Japan Institute, later renamed for him.
caveat: Born and raised in Tokyo to American missionary parents.

name: Mike Mansfield
did: After 34 years in Congress, including as Senate majority leader, he served as US ambassador to Japan from 1977 to 1988 under Presidents Carter and Reagan.

name: Nicholas Roerich
did: The St Petersburg-born painter lived in India from 1923, founded the Urusvati Himalayan Research Institute in Kullu (1928), and developed the Roerich Pact, the first international treaty to protect cultural property.
src: Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts
caveat: Also lived in New York in the 1920s; his Central Asian expeditions were controversial.

name: Lu Xun
did: Studied medicine at Sendai Medical College (now Tohoku University) under Fujino Genkurō, a friendship that became a symbol of China–Japan ties, marked by a Lu Xun memorial in Sendai since 1960.
caveat: Lived in Japan 1902–1909 overall; the Sendai period was 1904–1906.

name: Okakura Kakuzō
did: Stayed with Rabindranath Tagore's family in India (1901–1902), where he drafted 'The Ideals of the East', and from 1904 built the Asian art collection at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
caveat: His 'Asia is one' idea was later used in Japanese imperial propaganda.

name: Kōnosuke Matsushita
did: Hosted Deng Xiaoping at his factory in 1978 and pledged help with China's modernisation, leading to Beijing Matsushita Color CRT (1987), then the largest China–Japan joint venture.
src: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the PRC
